transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Dana Park (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood Product), Rachel Martin (Lynx Head of ML), Kunal Shah (Platform Eng), Priya Suresh (CTO), Tom Lee (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Walkthrough of Optimize playbook for batching and cache (prefix/KV) with example cost model. Action: send playbook + sandbox setup.

---
[00:00] Samir: okay everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Samir from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me is Dana our systems SE and Lena from product who will walk through the Optimize playbook. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Rachel: good, thanks, excited to get into the econ side, we've been running some rough numbers and want a pragmatic plan for our chat use case.
[00:10] Kunal: quick ask — we want recommendations we can implement in 2 sprints; also we need to see the impact on our cost run-rate, not just theoretical.
[00:16] Samir: totally. goal for today is a playbook synthesis: give you an ordered set of levers — batching, prefix + KV caching, sessionization, and routing — and show a small cost model that maps to your traffic. then we propose a 14-day sandbox so you can validate with your traces. sound right?
[00:25] Priya: yes, and include fallback behavior; we can't have the app degrade to huge latency if cache misses spike.
[00:29] Dana: absolutely, we'll show fallback policies (reserved capacity + model variant routing) and how to set TTLs and prefetch heuristics to avoid cold storm.

[05:12] Dana: okay quick context — from what Rachel shared we saw short multi-turn chats, average prompt tokens ~180, average generation tokens ~60, peak RPS ~65 for a single region — that's the sample you gave last week. does that still look right?
[05:24] Rachel: yes that's the sample, 95th p95 latency target is 250ms for interactive flows, and we target below $X per active session monthly — (laughter) we'll, we'll share the concrete budget number after this call.
[05:34] Tom: our SRE note: we want predictable 95th, and we prefer reserved pool for production if it makes sense economically.

[07:02] Dana: alright, first lever: batching. there's micro-batching (send small batches every 20–40ms) vs macro batching (wait longer to form big batches). micro keeps latency tight, macro improves token unit cost. here's a simple model:
- Baseline (no batching): tokens processed per request = 240 average, cost per million tokens with model M-1 = $Y (note: placeholder)
- Micro-batching (20–40ms): average batch size 3–5 requests, latency adds ~15–40ms at tail, cost reduction ~25–35% depending on concurrency.
- Macro-batching (100–200ms): batch size 12–30, latency increases 100–180ms, cost reduction up to 60% but fails 95th latency for you.

[07:45] Rachel: okay so for us micro-batching is probably more acceptable; we have interactive UX. can you show how that ties to KV cache?
[07:53] Dana: yes — second lever: prefix and KV caching. two patterns: prefix (session prefix cache) where common opening prompts or user profile context are cached as KV that the runtime can reuse as a keyed prefix; and per-session KV for longer conversational state. hit rate assumptions matter — with 60% hit-rate on prefixes you get huge token savings (you avoid re-sending repeated content).

[09:10] Kunal: what's the right TTL? we don't want to keep stale user data too long.
[09:14] Lena: TTL usually maps to session semantics. for short chat sessions TTL 5–15 minutes gives good hit-rate without holding stale info. we often suggest sliding TTL with access refresh: if session receives new turns, extend TTL.

[10:05] Dana: here's an example cost table we walked through in the playbook (Dana shares screen — link in notes):
- Raw tokens/unit (no cache) per session = 240 tokens -> monthly tokens = 240 * active_sessions * avg_sessions/month.
- With prefix cache hit-rate 50% and batch size 4, effective tokens served drops by ~55% -> unit cost halves roughly.
- Add KV sessionization (hot session cache) with hit-rate 80% on mid-session turns -> additional 10–25% savings.

[12:40] Rachel: do you account for extra memory cost on the nodes for KV storage? we're concerned about memory spike during peak.
[12:48] Dana: yes we model memory & lookup cost as a small per-lookup CPU/RAM overhead. in Redwood Optimize we recommend sizing cache TTLs so hot keys live in GPU memory-friendly stores or low-latency RAM cache (not on disk). if you need, we can route cache-heavy traffic to dedicated pool to isolate memory footprint. that's what Dedicated does.

[14:11] Tom: about failure modes — if cache store is overloaded and lookups start failing, does runtime fall back to sending full prompt?
[14:19] Dana: default is fail-open: if cache lookup fails, request falls back to full prompt on primary model variant. we can also configure graceful degrade: route to cheaper smaller quantized variant with slightly higher latency but lower cost, or queue micro-batches to smooth bursts.

[16:02] Samir: quick note on model routing: for many customers we route repetitive system prompts to a lower-capacity quantized model for cost savings, and rare/novel queries to full-precision model. helps maintain quality while saving tokens and compute.

[18:55] Kunal: show me sensitivity: if our prefix hit-rate is actually 30% vs 50%, how badly do numbers change?
[19:03] Dana: good question — in the spreadsheet Dana posts (link) we model three scenarios: pessimistic 30% hit, baseline 50%, optimistic 70%. sample result: with micro-batching at concurrency 10 and model M-1 pricing:
- 30% hit -> ~28% cost reduction vs baseline
- 50% hit -> ~45% cost reduction
- 70% hit -> ~60% cost reduction
So the playbook recommends focusing on improving prefix hit through deterministic session keys and client-side sticky routing.

[21:40] Rachel: we have fairly predictable session patterns for new users vs returning; maybe we can precompute prefixes for returning users. how invasive is that on client?
[21:50] Dana: minimal — you add a session key in the request, Redwood Optimize console can accept prefetch events (we call them lookahead events) to prime the KV cache before the user arrives. client needs to emit small prefetch webhook or event, or server-side job can precompute.

[24:12] Priya: what about TTL's effect on cost—do shorter TTLs cause more backend writes and thus higher overhead?
[24:19] Lena: yes TTL churn increases write rate; that's why we recommend a hybrid: short TTL for non-critical user state and longer sliding TTL for more stable prefixes. the cost model includes a small per-write charge; it's dwarfed by token cost, but it's visible in high-churn workloads.

[26:00] Dana: next lever — concurrency and batch shaping. we recommend shaping client concurrency so that the runtime forms steady micro-batches. too spiky and you miss batching opportunities; too slow and UX suffers. we often set a concurrency cap client-side and use token-based throttles with backpressure.

[28:30] Tom: how do we validate in sandbox? can Redwood simulate our traffic shape?
[28:36] Samir: yes sandbox will let you replay traces to our Optimize simulator and run the same hit-rate scenarios. we'll provide a cost-run CSV with scenario toggles you can flip to see cost and latency tradeoffs.

[30:45] Kunal: show me an explicit policy: if 95th latency > 350ms, funnel to reserved pool or route to model variant?
[30:52] Dana: we recommend tiered fallback: primary path is hosted optimized model with micro-batching + prefix cache. if p95 crosses threshold, trigger routing policy to reserved capacity (if you have Dedicated) or to quantized variant with automatic quality regression alert. also set canary + auto-fallthrough to avoid hard errors. we can demo the console rule later.

[33:15] Rachel: any gotchas on metrics? what should our observability track to be confident?
[33:22] Lena: track these key metrics: cache hit-rate (prefix & session), avg batch size, p50/p95 generation latency, token consumption per session, and fallback rate (percent routed to smaller variant). set regression alerts on QoQ changes. Redwood Console surfaces token-level cost and per-route latency.

[35:40] Kunal: quick question on encryption/KMS: if we prefetch user profile into KV cache, how is that encrypted at rest?
[35:47] Dana: the private deployment or Dedicated option supports KMS integration and HSM key wrapping; for hosted we use tenant encryption and can integrate your KMS for key rotation in Private deployments. we'll include security docs (SOC2, ISO summary) in the package.

[37:00] Tom: what about data residency? some of our EU users must keep data in region.
[37:07] Samir: we can pin routing by region and provide Private or VPC deployment if you need full data residency and isolation. that's part of the next-step discussion.

[38:45] Rachel: can you walk through a short worked example — give me numbers for a single active user session and monthly run-rate using our baseline and improved playbook?
[38:52] Dana: sure — quick worked example on screen (Dana posts simple calc):
- Baseline: avg tokens/session = 240, avg sessions/day per active user = 3, active users 10k -> monthly tokens ~240 * 3 * 10k * 30 = 216M tokens -> cost (model M-1) = $A (placeholder)
- With micro-batching (x3) and prefix hit 50%: effective tokens -> ~95M tokens -> cost falls roughly ~56% vs baseline.
- With additional session KV hit 80% on mid-turns -> tokens ~72M -> further 10–15% savings.
Note: these numbers depend heavily on hit-rate and batch sizes; the spreadsheet has toggles.

[42:10] Kunal: any impact on token counting accuracy with KV? do we still get transparent per-token logs?
[42:16] Lena: yes token accounting remains transparent; when prefix is reused we show synthetic token reduction in the console and break down tokens saved by cache vs batching. auditing remains intact for billing.

[44:30] Rachel: okay what's the simplest pilot to prove this for us in 2 weeks?
[44:36] Samir: recommended pilot: 1) Redwood provisions sandbox project with replay of 3 days of your live trace; 2) enable micro-batching at 30ms window + prefix cache with TTL 10 minutes; 3) run three scenarios (30/50/70% hit) and capture p95 latency and cost delta; 4) Redwood provides annotated CSV and playbook recommendations.
[45:05] Priya: timeline — when can you start?
[45:08] Dana: we can spin up sandbox infra this week once we get the traces and a quick infra contact, Kunal?
[45:14] Kunal: i'll share S3 sample traces plus our schema tonight.

[47:50] Samir: great. last thing — I want to call out a few tradeoffs we wrote into the playbook:
- Aggressive TTLs and long prefetching improve hits but increase memory and complexity.
- Larger batches reduce per-token cost but increase p95 latency.
- Dedicated pools remove noisy neighbor risk but come with commit cost.

[49:05] Rachel: yep, understood. we'll review the spreadsheet and replay and then align on pilot metrics.

[50:20] Dana: i'll follow up with the Optimize playbook PDF and the cost spreadsheet link. (screen link posted) Link: https://redwood.local/optimize/playbooks/lynx-playbook-2026-10-07.pdf (internal link)

[50:50] Samir: recap of next steps — I will send the playbook + spreadsheet; Dana will provision sandbox and invite Kunal/Tom; Priya/Rachel will share traces and budget constraints. schedule kickoff for the pilot next week.

[51:10] Rachel: thanks team, that was helpful.
[51:16] Tom: thanks, bye.
[51:20] Samir: thanks everyone, talk soon.
